destination.title: Your Home for a Developer? The Kelo Supreme Court Case

short10: The government can take your home, in perfect condition, and hand the land to a private developer.
In 2005, in New London, Connecticut, one woman's little pink house was perfectly fine.
But the city wanted offices and a hotel, for jobs and taxes.
The Constitution allows taking property for public use.
In 2005, the Supreme Court said yes, five to four.
But the project was never built.
The land sat empty for years.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: The Constitution allows takings "for public use." Is handing your home to a private developer — for a plan that might create jobs — really a "public use"?
"Public use," in other words, would be read as "public purpose." One vote in the majority came with a caveat.
"Passed a reform" did not always mean "actually protected homeowners" .
In 2005, a woman's small pink house in Connecticut put that exact question in front of the Supreme Court .
So the case was never really about one pink house.
In 2005, the Supreme Court sided with the city.
Because the public reaction to Kelo did something American legal decisions almost never do: it united nearly everyone against it.
After the homes of Fort Trumbull were taken and demolished, the grand redevelopment was never built.
In 2009, Pfizer — the company whose arrival had justified the whole plan — closed its New London facility and left .
The neighborhood had been erased for a development that never came, to serve a company that did not stay.
The Supreme Court has never overturned it.
era_note: SET THIS. Modern stock footage is only usable if the case is modern; a 1960s case dressed in present-day footage reads wrong.

shorts.angle: Justice O'Connor's dissent is the part nobody quotes: after Kelo, any home could be taken for any private use that promised more tax revenue than the house did.
shorts.type: C — a quotation or document (the dissent)
shorts.avoids: The existing Short tells the pink-house story, the five to four vote and the empty lot. It never says what the four dissenters argued, or that the logic reaches any modest house that generates less revenue than what a developer would put there.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: What the country did about the ruling afterward, and why forty state reforms changed less than people assume.
shorts.loop_join: L5 leaves the majority rule in force, so L1 comes back as that rule applied to your own house rather than as a hypothetical.

lines.text: Your house produces less tax revenue than a hotel. After 2005, that alone could justify taking it.
source_lines: A modest house almost always produces less tax revenue than offices or luxury condos. Under the broad reading, that gap alone could justify taking it

lines.text: The Court read for public use as public purpose. A development plan aimed at jobs and revenue counts, and courts should defer to the city.
source_lines: It said that a carefully considered economic-development plan, aimed at public benefits like jobs and revenue, qualifies as a public purpose — and that courts should largely defer to a city's judgment about what its community needs
"Public use," in other words, would be read as "public purpose."

lines.text: Justice Sandra Day O'Connor wrote the main dissent. The government, she warned, could now take property from one private owner simply to give it to another who might use it more profitably.
source_lines: Justice Sandra Day O'Connor wrote the main dissent, and her warning was blunt.
Under this ruling, she argued, the government could now take property from one private owner simply to give it to another who might use it more profitably.

lines.text: The specter, she wrote, was that any home could be taken for any other private use that promised more taxes. That for public use had, in effect, been erased from the Constitution.
source_lines: The specter, she wrote, was that any home could be taken for any other private use that promised more taxes — and that the words "for public use" had, in effect, been erased from the Constitution

lines.text: Justice Thomas wrote a separate dissent, arguing the Court had drifted far from the original meaning of the clause.
source_lines: Justice Thomas wrote a separate dissent arguing the Court had drifted far from the original meaning of the clause.

lines.text: One vote in the majority came with a caveat. Kennedy wrote separately that a merely pretextual public purpose would still be unconstitutional.
source_lines: One vote in the majority came with a caveat.

Justice Kennedy, who joined the Court's opinion, wrote separately to stress that a taking meant only to benefit a particular private party, with a merely pretextual public purpose, would still be unconstitutional

lines.text: It was five to four, and unlike many such splits it did not fall along the usual lines.
source_lines: It was a 5-4 split, and unlike many such splits, it did not fall along the usual lines.

lines.text: Her warning was a dissent, which means it never became the law. The majority's rule is the one still standing.

shorts.angle: Roughly forty states rewrote their eminent domain laws after Kelo and many of those reforms were criticised as hollow, while the company whose arrival justified the whole plan closed up and left in 2009.

shorts.avoids: The existing Short ends at 'the project was never built, the land sat empty'. It never mentions the reform wave, how weak those reforms were said to be, or that Pfizer left New London four years after the homes came down.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: What happened to Susette Kelo's pink house itself.

lines.text: Dozens of state legislatures rushed to fix this. Many of those laws were criticized as hollow.
source_lines: In the years after Kelo, by the Institute for Justice's count, roughly forty or more states passed new laws or constitutional amendments restricting the use of eminent domain for economic development.
many of these reforms were later criticized as weak, full of loopholes that left the core power largely intact

lines.text: The ruling set off one of the largest backlashes to any modern Supreme Court decision, and a rare bipartisan one. Legislatures responded fast.
source_lines: The ruling set off one of the largest popular backlashes to any modern Supreme Court decision — and a rare bipartisan one.
And legislatures responded.

lines.text: Roughly forty or more states passed new laws restricting eminent domain for economic development. But many were later criticized as weak, full of loopholes.
source_lines: In the years after Kelo, by the Institute for Justice's count, roughly forty or more states passed new laws or constitutional amendments restricting the use of eminent domain for economic development.

lines.text: In 2009, Pfizer, the company whose arrival had justified the whole plan, closed its New London facility and left. A neighborhood erased for a development that never came, to serve a company that did not stay.
source_lines: In 2009, Pfizer — the company whose arrival had justified the whole plan — closed its New London facility and left

lines.text: The city never claimed Fort Trumbull was a slum, and the Court did not say the homes had to be blighted.
source_lines: The city was not claiming Fort Trumbull was a slum.
The Court did not say the homes had to be blighted.

lines.text: Some families had lived there for generations. They were paid market value, which does not buy back a lifetime in one place.
source_lines: Some families had been in Fort Trumbull for generations.

They were paid the market value of their homes, as the Constitution requires — but market value does not buy back the place you have lived your whole life, or the neighbors who scatter once the bulldozers arrive.

lines.text: For a long time the most famous use of the bulldozed land was as a place to dump storm debris.

lines.text: The houses were gone, the company was gone, and the ruling still stood. Which raises the obvious question of what anyone did about it.
